analysis.one_liner: Exempts dirt bikes, ATVs, and snowmobiles from children's product lead-content limits.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 70 cosponsors that would lift the lead-content ban on youth-model off-road vehicles never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2008 consumer safety law set strict lead limits for products aimed at children, and the rules ended up covering youth-model dirt bikes, ATVs, and snowmobiles, because their metal parts contain small amounts of lead. This bill would have permanently exempted those vehicles from the lead limits. It would also have made it easier for the Consumer Product Safety Commission to grant exemptions for other products, changing the test from products with no lead absorption at all to products where lead is not absorbed into the body.
analysis.who_benefits: Families in rural and snow-belt areas who buy youth-model dirt bikes, ATVs, and snowmobiles for their kids, and the manufacturers that sell them. The 2008 law's lead limits effectively blocked sales of youth-model machines because small amounts of lead are present in metal components like engines and brakes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural families and off-road vehicle makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act of 2008 so its lead limits no longer apply to off-highway vehicles, defined as any straddle-seat, handlebar-steered motorized vehicle on two, three, or four wheels, plus snowmobiles.
It would restore access to youth-model machines that families could no longer buy under the lead rules, keeping children off full-size adult vehicles that are harder for them to control.

The bill also loosens the standard the Commission uses to exempt other products from the lead limits, from products where no lead is absorbed into the body to products where lead will not be absorbed, making exemptions easier to obtain across the board.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the strength of the children's lead-safety standard. Exempting vehicles removes the limit that applied to their parts, and the broader change to the exemption standard would make it easier for makers of any children's product to win relief from the limits. Pediatric health advocates argue there is no safe level of lead exposure for children.

drawbacks.text: The exemption removes lead-content limits from products used by children, and the bill also weakens the general exemption standard for every other children's product, taking a rule created after the 2007 lead-tainted toy recalls and carving exceptions into it.
The exemption is written broadly: it covers any two-, three-, or four-wheeled straddle-seat motorized vehicle, not just youth models, so adult machines used by children are also swept in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill is practical: the lead in these vehicles sits in engine and brake components that children do not mouth or touch the way they touch toys, and the ban took youth machines off the market, which can push kids onto adult-sized vehicles that fit them worse. The honest objection is that the bill does not merely fix that narrow problem; it also lowers the bar for exemptions from the lead rules generally, which weakens the very standard that was enacted to protect children after the toy-recall scandal. A narrower exemption tied to youth models would have balanced the two concerns better.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to committee and then to a subcommittee within two days of introduction, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rehberg and three colleagues introduced the bill on March 18, 2009, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it remained without action.
It attracted 70 cosponsors from both parties, 47 Republicans and 23 Democrats, but the committee never scheduled a markup or hearing.
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Backers of strict children's lead-safety standards are better off that the bill died, since the lead limits on off-road vehicles and the strict exemption standard both stayed in force. But families also gained nothing: youth-model off-road machines remained barred under the rules as written, a problem that stayed unresolved when this Congress ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Child lead-safety advocates; families got no relief

for.name: Denny Rehberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt off-highway vehicles from the lead limits.

for.name: 23 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Pomeroy and Burgess's fellow original cosponsor list.

for.name: Off-highway vehicle industry
for.what_they_did: Backed the exemption after the 2008 lead rules halted youth-model ATV and dirt bike sales.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or hearing during the two years it sat on the committee's docket.

against.name: Bobby Rush
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 19, 2009 and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was clearly bipartisan with 47 Republicans and 23 Democrats cosponsoring, but no one ever voted on it, so the partisan shape of the inaction was never tested.

industries.note: The bill restores the ability to sell youth-model ATVs, dirt bikes, and snowmobiles that the 2008 lead rules effectively pulled off the market, benefiting makers and the families who buy their products together.

The bill's second change lowers the bar for any product maker to win an exemption from the children's lead limits, weakening a rule adopted after the lead-tainted toy recalls, and that relief comes at the expense of the lead-safety standard children rely on.
Exempting off-highway vehicles and easing the exemption standard reduces the volume of mandatory lead testing children's products must undergo.
